7.11.m:
"Who are you in the form of a boar here, having crossed the swelling sea?
Why have you come here, or where are you to go?" (9)
Hearing their words, that high-minded Boar,
resembling the rumble of a raincloud, then said to all the Dānavas: (10)
"I am a boar, O Daityas, as you can see by such a form.
I have come to this region for roaming about, without a doubt. (11)
My wife has been abducted by another; despondent, O foremost of Daityas,
I am wandering about, contemplating the recovery of that villain's spoils." (12)
The Dānavas said:
"This is not a wandering ground for you; this is the realm of the Daityas.
Disregarding the Daityas, how have you come into this land? (13)
We shall kill you today, all of us, lowest of the race of beasts!
And having slain you, we will indeed take you before the lord of the Daityas." (14)
Then all those Dānavas struck him violently with excellent weapons,
just as haughty clouds [strike] a mountain with rain. (15)
That strong, divine-souled Boar of exceedingly great might,
even while being struck, addressed these words to those Daityas: (16)
"Indeed, O best of Asuras, I have not committed even the slightest
offense against you here, nor will I do so, nor do I now. (17)"

There is no enmity between you and me here, nor indeed have you any business with me. (18)"
"If you have need of flesh, then strike me, O Dānavas,

exerting themselves vehemently, struck him with various missiles and weapons in hand. (23)

as a tiger by deer, as a lion by hares, (24)

even so was that blessed Boar who increases joy, O Vyāsa. (25)
Tormented by them, taking no heed, he stood like an immovable mountain.

and many others such as these, the lord of beasts was being struck,
he became invisible, and then they all rejoiced greatly. (27)

7.11.m:
Having slain all those servants, he came to the city of the Aśmakas, / roaring like a cloud pouring down rain at the end of an era.
Having gone to that city, O Vyāsa, the almighty lord, consisting of all worlds, / turning from left to right, arrived at the southern gate.
There, by the many Danavas guarding the southern gate, / an exceedingly loud clamour was raised, by which the city was agitated.
For, having shattered the *śataghnī*s, the door panels, and the heavy clubs, / that imperishable one ground to powder the wheels of destruction and the siege engines.
Then, filled with intense rage, those Danava great car-warriors arrived, / covering the lord of beasts with a fierce shower of weapons.
Then, struck by them with javelins, discuses, and *bhindipāla* slings, / he abandoned the gate, came forth, and took his stand on level ground.
Thinking then, 'He is defeated indeed!', those Asuras, O Vyāsa, / pursued him from behind, hacking at him with their choice weapons.
Being hacked by the downpour of arrows, javelins, massive clubs, and iron-tipped pestles, / having come out then, he, abode of the hosts of the gods, fought the sons of Diti.
Thus ends the one hundred and second chapter, entitled 'The Encounter with the Asuras', in the Skandapurāṇa.

'Have you no shame, O lords of Danavas, in coming to battle? / Or perhaps you have no strength, and it was falsely that you conquered the gods!
You are many and strong, while I am a beast of the forest; / I do not think, O best of Danavas, that your mind is set on righteous combat.
I have no bow whatsoever, nor any weapon of that kind, / by which I might fight against many armed ones, O lords of Asuras.
If you agree, cast down your weapons now, / and fight with me one by one, adhering to the rules of fair combat.'
Sanatkumāra said: / Hearing that speech of his, Andhaka, the lord of the Danavas, / spoke to all the Daitya leaders, roaring like a cloud at the end of an era:
'It is just as this beast has said, O great Daitya car-warriors! / Let us cast away our weapons today, and fight one by one!'
Prahlāda said: / 'This is folly, O lords of Daityas, just as this vile beast has spoken! / A battle is praised when it is between equals with equals.
Beasts possess neither weapons nor the strength of arms; / yet they are ever slain with weapons: this is considered the law by the righteous.
How can we, O lords of Danavas, abandon our own duty, / adopt the ways of beasts, and fight like animals?
This vile, wicked beast is not unfit to be killed by us and our kind. / […] Let there be no hesitation whatsoever on your part regarding this beast!
Employing sorcery, this wicked-souled defiler of the gods, / full of evil intent, wishes to deceive us, O Daityas!

'Where has it been heard or seen, O lords of Asuras, / that beasts engage in wrestling with men in battle, like human beings?
This is Viṣṇu of wicked conduct, evil-souled, a thorn to the Daityas, / who, incapable through his own valour, stands here resorting to illusion.'
Sanatkumāra said: / Then that powerful lord of Asuras, enraged, O Vyāsa, covered him / with many arrows from his bow and shouted fiercely.
Andhaka, Vipracitti, and all those Daityas and Danavas / showered him with sharp arrows by the hundreds and thousands.
Then the divine one, pierced exceedingly by those deeply enraged Danavas, / shone like Mount Himālaya covered with the rays of the sun.
Gathering powerful speed, shaking off the sharp arrows, / the lord playfully advanced against the Danava Prahlāda.
Having rushed to his chariot, he forthwith reduced the charioteer and the chariot / to mere names by means of his tusks and forelegs.
Then, springing down from the chariot though struck by the Danavas, / the god struck that Daitya on the head with the chariot's banner-pole.
Prahlāda, too, leaping up then with a club of dreadful appearance, / struck the enraged one on the chest, like an obstacle standing in the way of righteousness.
Struck by him, the god abandoned his chariot then, / and returned to that very place where he had stood previously.
Then Andhaka, Vipracitti, Śambara, and Kālaśambara / pierced Nandivardhana with arrows resembling venomous serpents.

Sanatkumāra said:
Then, having given orders to his charioteer, he had his chariot made ready. / To console his wives, he entered his apartments again. / Performed auspicious rites by them there at that time, and having looked upon those sons of Diti all around, / the mighty one took up all the radiant gear suitable for battle, capable of warding off enemies. / Thus ends the one hundred and fourth chapter in the Skandapurāṇa, in the Fall of Vipracitti.

Sanatkumāra said:
Thus nourished, O Vyāsa, powerful and possessing the radiance of the sun, / he moved around in diverse, many, and swift circles.
Making leaps like a lion, he looked at once / behind and ahead, and again acted like an elephant.
Again opening his mouth wide, he swallowed the enemy's weapons; / again with trees and rocks he slaughtered the dānavas.
Again moving through the sky, he flew about like the king of birds; / again, enraged, he laughed like the crash of a thunderbolt;
and again making himself minute, he then stood before him. / Seeing him thus leaping and roaring, the dānava / Hiraṇyākṣa, his face knit with frowns, spoke, making the space resound: / "O vile beast, foolish one, you shall not escape!
Having slain you by my might, I will offer you as an oblation to Rudra. / By you, wicked-souled one, was my elder brother slain through deceit; / of that deed, O evil-souled one, the fruit has come upon you today!"
Sanatkumāra said:
Hearing those words of Hiraṇyākṣa in battle, / the blessed Lord Viṣṇu spoke, enraging the son of Diti:
"That mighty daitya was slain by me as Narasiṃha, / having displayed prowess in battle; likewise your slaying is certain!
Whether you go to the sky, or into Pātāla, or even beyond, / or to a mountain or to the ocean, even so you shall not be freed!"

Once more I shall slay you, like a lion a deer in the open plain!
What power have you here today, without the boon from Maheśvara,

Assuming a body made of the worlds, presided over by them,

even so, you are not able [to face] me today, just as a deer cannot face a lion,

One who is noble, learned, and established on the path of the good,
thinking himself defeated by such a one, would abandon the fight.

with palms, with fists, with arms, with feet, / with claws, with teeth, and with other [moves], the two of mighty strength. / Thus the battle between the two, god and daitya, went on / for ten and eight days, and then for another fourteen, / and another thousand human years. / Such was the time spent there; then the daitya lost his strength.

7.11.m: “Listen, O divine Boar, to this, and having heard it, act accordingly! / For this daitya of mighty strength cannot be killed by you in this way. / This cruel one has surely been rendered powerless by the energy / of the Great Lord; look at him: this is his time. / Release this king of the daityas and destroy him with the discus; / through the energy of the Great Lord, O Vaikuṇṭha, he will then meet his death.” / Sanatkumāra said: / Then, having heard that, the Blessed One, the promoter of joy, / released the king of the daityas, striking him on the chest with his foot. / Released by that god, that bull among daityas shone resplendent, / like the sun devoured and released by the son of Siṃhikā, Rāhu. / The Blessed One too, seeing that daitya blazing with splendor, / bowed to Pinākin and remembered that discus. / Then all the directions, O Vyāsa, glowed like fire-pits, / and there was an immense sound resembling the clouds at the end of the age. / The siddhas fell to the earth, and fear seized the gods. / “May there be well-being for all beings!” the sages then proclaimed. / The oceans dried up, and the serpents and birds perished; / the daityas and dānavas all entered subterranean chasms. / Beings were terrified with fear, and meteors fell from the vault of the sky, / as that exceedingly radiant discus, like the fire at the end of the age, arrived— / that great razor-edged discus, ending aquatic creatures that plunge into waters, / dreadful to behold, destroying everything, impenetrable, and counter-striking.

7.11.m: Thus irresistible, divine, bewildering all embodied beings, / roaring like a hundred thunderbolts, it reached the Boar's hand. / Seeing it descending, all creatures on all sides / fell to the ground, terrified, and could see nothing at all. / Then that god, having assumed an immense, imperishable form / pervading the three worlds, hurled [it] toward the dānava, making [the worlds] resound. / Resembling the fire at the end of the age, razor-edged, tearing open the sky, / it sped quickly toward the dānava, as if burning all the quarters. / That tiger among dānavas, unflinching, O son of Śakti, / struck the approaching [discus] of mighty roar with diverse missiles. / But that great fire-like discus reduced those missiles / to ashes, O Vyāsa, and advanced, roaring aloud. / Then [the dānava] unleashed illusion: fiery and earthy, / airy, watery, dark, and sensual, / and similarly illusion of portents, bewildering, paralyzing, / turning away, crushing, and produced others in the battle. / Then that terribly roaring discus destroyed all of them, / went and severed his head from his body, like a mountain[-peak]. / That very great, supreme head severed by it, with gaping mouth and fierce eyes like fire, / bearing great tusks, with a wondrous and dreadful roar, fell like a lofty peak of Meru. / Its form drained of vitality by the wheel-weapon, that face, devoid of color, did not shine, appearing utterly wretched, / like the disc of the moon stripped of splendor at daybreak when its rays have ceased.

Sanatkumāra said:
When that Daitya was slain, all the gods sang praises;
and the seers endowed with austerity showered down rains of flowers. // 1
Unseen celestial drums of immense sound resounded;
there was peace for living beings, and the world regained its natural order. // 2

and the seers and the worlds saw that Daitya slain. // 3
All those Asuras as well, having closed the city gates on every side
with diligence, stood fully armed upon the ramparts. // 4
Terrified, their hair disheveled, covered with dust and afflicted by fear,
anxious to preserve their lives, they remained standing on the ramparts. // 5
The Lord too, blazing with flames like a fire fueled with clarified butter,
terrifying all the Asuras, searched for the earth. // 6
Searching everywhere outside and uprooting trees,
he sought all around, like a cowherd looking for a lost cow. // 7

he smashed groves and reservoirs and let out a mighty roar. // 8

circumambulated him and went away to their respective abodes. // 22

having slain the foremost of Dānavas, sported happily there. // 23

7.11.m: Sanatkumāra said: / As he was sporting thus for a long time, O son of Śakti, / a son named Vṛka was born to his wife Citralekhā. // That Vṛka, always mighty, wandering over this earth / and roaring, slew hundreds of living beings in the world, being huge. // Then he reached the king of mountains, the great Himavat mountain, / and near the peak of Gaurī, the auspicious abode of Kārtikeya. // Not knowing it, he approached with violence and insolence, / shaking the radiant trees adorned with gems and gold, // that bore fruit and flowers in all seasons and granted all desires, / radiant with jewel-stones and made of gold, // and other rocks of yellow orpiment and realgar; / tearing them up with speed, he broke them as if enraged. // Roaring continuously like another rutting elephant, / he shattered that splendid grove belonging to wise Kārtikeya. // At the sound of his roaring and the crash of the grove being destroyed, / a heroic leader of Skanda's attendants came out from the dwelling.

Then out of anger, blazing fire came forth from his eyes / as if destroying the entire world with its radiance.
Rising at once from his seat, looking upward with fiery gaze, / the god himself, the lion of beasts, departed for Gaurī's divine peak.
Making the whole earth tremble, praised by high-souled beings, / he went unrestrained, seeing rising omens of calamity.
As that god went on his way, a serpent bit [him], / and a tusk struck a tree and fell to the surface of the earth.
Blood flowed from his mouth, and his heart trembled violently; / fear came upon him there, whereby his swift pace was impeded.
Adverse winds blew, and he fell on the ground upon his chest; / remembering his beloved, affection arose exceedingly in him then.
Disregarding these and many other omens that indicated danger, / that mighty beast-king went straight on, possessed of great power.
Seeing him depart, and observing the omens, O one of noble vows, / the denizens of heaven prepared an offering in the realm of the gods.
Followed by hosts of Siddhas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and great serpents, / by troops of Rākṣasas, Cāraṇas, and Kinnaras, that great soul went to Gaurī's peak.
Thus ends the hundred and ninth chapter, named the Binding of Vṛka, in the Skandapurāṇa.

Taking a huge rock, enraged like the god of death, / roaring like a rain-cloud, he hurled it at Kārttikeya.
As it came flying through the sky with an appearance like death itself, roaring repeatedly, / Kokāmukha swiftly caught that extremely swift [rock] like a blazing meteor.
Then the lord unleashed his thousand-spoked discus, radiant as the fire at the end of an aeon, / against Vināyaka's unperturbed troop.
That discus resembling Death, the slayer of all the enemies of the gods, / entered [among them]; the troop quickly [fell back], and then it turned away.
That discus, having returned without accomplishing its brilliant task, / was not received back by Viṣṇu, who then felt disregarded by it.
Unwelcomed by that Viṣṇu, the slayer of Dānavas, / the discus swiftly returned to its own abode.
When that discus had departed, the divine increaser of joy / uprooted a tree with speed and struck Kumāra.

7.11.m:
Whoever, O goddesses, O auspicious ones, gives food—of whatever kind—
even to him, when he is being tormented by rākṣasas in a terrible hell,
sustenance comes in abundance, whereby satisfaction arises for him.
If at some point that man returns to human existence,
he becomes an enjoyer of pleasures among the mlecchas and rejoices like an immortal.
Food alone is thus superior; therefore, there is nothing higher on earth.
Food is declared to be Prajāpati, and he is considered to be the year;
and the year is that sacrifice, [and] everything is established in the sacrifice.
From that arise beings, both stationary and moving.
Therefore, food is indeed superior to all—so says the sacred tradition.
There is indeed no gift higher than the gift of food.
From food beings arise; therefore, that is indeed praised.

Sweet-smelling, cool water endowed with divine flavors—
hear the reward of his giving who offers it to brahmins:
Mounting an aerial chariot resembling the sun and filled with the music of apsarases,
he goes to heaven, achieving dwelling in the world of Varuṇa.
Having dwelt there for eighty thousand [years], happy like a god,
he is born in a great, unmixed family, rich in wealth and grain.
He who gives a vessel full of water to a brahmin—
flavors attend him, and, having gone to heaven, he is honored.
